channel.title: Pawan Sinha — Blog
channel.description: Deep dives on performance engineering, load testing and capacity planning.

item.title: Your fan-out turns a 1% slow call into 63% slow requests
item.description: The maths of tail latency under fan-out from Dean and Barroso's "The Tail at Scale", why a back-end's p99 stops being good enough, and the fixes that work: hedged and tied requests, deadlines, fewer sequential hops and load tests that report per-call percentiles.

item.title: Your iostat says fine but writes stall for 500 ms
item.description: Why %util lies on SSDs and cloud volumes, how to read await and aqu-sz with Little's Law, why per-second averages hide stalls, what fsync and writeback really cost, and how gp2 burst credits make short load tests pass.

item.title: Your 1% trace sample threw away the slow requests
item.description: Head sampling keeps 1% of everything, including 1% of the requests you actually need to debug. How to keep every slow and failed trace, link metrics to traces with exemplars, and close the loop with logs and profiles.

item.title: Your HPA decided in 15 seconds. Capacity took three minutes
item.description: Scale-out lag is rarely the HPA's maths. It is metric delay, scale-up policies, node provisioning and pod start time stacked together. What the stabilisation window really does, how to size the backlog a ramp creates, and how to test it with an arrival-rate load test.

item.title: The load tool you picked by habit can't test gRPC
item.description: Most teams pick a load tool by habit and find its limits mid-project. A fair comparison of k6, JMeter, Gatling, Locust and LoadRunner on the constraints that actually block you: protocol, workload model, language, scale-out cost and result fidelity.

item.title: Every GC pause met the goal. p99.9 still failed.
item.description: A pause-time goal says how long each pause may be, not how many requests it hits. How allocation rate and eden size set pause frequency, what really drives G1, ZGC and Shenandoah tail latency, and how to prove it from unified GC logs.

item.title: Green load test, red production: finding the database bottleneck
item.description: Why a PostgreSQL-backed service passes its load test and still blows its p99 in production, and the order I check things in: pool exhaustion, N+1, generic-plan flips, lock waits, replicas and indexes, with the exact queries for PostgreSQL 13+.

item.title: Your capacity plan breaks long before 100% utilisation
item.description: Why response time bends upward long before a server is full, how Kingman's formula prices the cost of bursty traffic, how many servers change the answer, and how to measure and load test the inputs.

item.title: When the cache fails, the database pays
item.description: Cache-aside, read-through, write-through and write-behind compared by failure mode, then the failures that matter at scale: stampedes, synchronised expiry, hot keys, cold starts, penetration, stale-write races and eviction churn.

item.title: The week-2 decisions that sink your week-38 load test
item.description: The cheapest performance work happens before anything is built. Measurable NFRs from business numbers, latency budgets per hop, a capacity model, an architecture risk review and a test strategy that grows with the system.

item.title: One GC pause, everyone's p99
item.description: Round robin assumes every request costs the same. It doesn't. Least outstanding requests, power of two choices, the connection-level imbalance that L4 hides, slow start, draining, and how to load test the balancer itself.

item.title: Why 500 threads made it slower
item.description: Size thread pools with Little's Law and the wait-to-compute ratio, bound queues by your latency budget, and read thread dumps for what threads are waiting on. Plus what changes with virtual threads.

item.title: Your load test is lying about p99
item.description: A closed-loop load generator politely waits whenever the system stalls, so the worst moments never get measured. A worked example, how to spot it in results you already have, and how to fix it.

item.title: One CDN purge can take down your origin
item.description: Origin load scales with (1 − hit ratio), cache keys quietly fragment, and synchronised expiry is a load test you never planned. How to engineer and test a CDN properly.

item.title: Your bottleneck isn't where you think it is
item.description: Most slow-system investigations start with a fix. Start instead with service demand, the USE method and a stepped open-model test, and prove the bottleneck before touching anything.
